title: Prince Ahmad and the Fairy Peri-Banu

keywords: prince ahmad and the fairy peri-banu
full_text:
In India ruled a mighty Sultan who had three sons: Prince Husayn, Prince Ali, and Prince Ahmad, alongside a beautiful orphaned niece, Princess Nur al-Nahar. All three brothers loved their cousin deeply.

To resolve their rivalry without bloodshed, the Sultan proclaimed:
'Travel to distant corners of the world. Whosoever brings back the most extraordinary curiosity shall have Nur al-Nahar as his bride.'

Prince Husayn traveled to the markets of Bishangar, where he purchased an enchanted tapestry: whoever sat upon it was transported instantaneously across mountains and seas to any destination desired.

Prince Ali traveled to Shiraz, where he acquired an ivory viewing-glass through which one could see any person or place in the world simply by wishing it.

Prince Ahmad journeyed to Samarkand, where he bought a magical artificial apple: inhaling its fragrance cured any mortal sickness instantly.

Meeting at an appointed caravanserai to compare their treasures, Prince Ali looked through his viewing-glass and cried in horror: 'Princess Nur al-Nahar lies dying in our father's palace!'
Prince Husayn spread his tapestry, all three leaped upon it, and arrived in the Princess's chamber in the twinkling of an eye! Prince Ahmad held the enchanted apple to her lips; she inhaled its healing fragrance and arose in perfect health!

The Sultan was in a dilemma: Ali's glass discovered the danger, Husayn's tapestry brought them in time, and Ahmad's apple cured her life. None was superior. He declared an archery contest: whoever shot his arrow farthest should win her hand.

Husayn shot far; Ali shot farther; but Ahmad's arrow flew so high and distant that none could find where it landed. Ali married Nur al-Nahar, while broken-hearted Husayn became a solitary hermit.

Ahmad, determined to find his arrow, wandered for days across rocky hills until he found the arrow lying far beyond possible human reach, near the foot of an iron cliff. Approaching, he found an iron door set in the mountain.

Entering, he was welcomed into a subterranean palace of crystal and jade by Peri-Banu, a powerful fairy princess. She revealed:
'Prince Ahmad, it was I who drew thy arrow across the sky. I have loved thee for thy gentleness and courage. If thou wilt accept my hand, my kingdom and devotion are thine.'

Ahmad gladly wed Peri-Banu, living in sublime happiness. Yet, missing his father, he obtained her permission to visit the Sultan with royal gifts, promising to return.

However, a wicked enchantress whispered poison into the Sultan's ear, suggesting Ahmad was amassing fairy armies to seize the throne. The Sultan, gripped by suspicion, demanded impossible tributes from Ahmad: first, a tent so vast it could shelter an entire army yet so light it could be held in the palm of a hand; then, water from the Fountain of Lions that cured all fevers; and finally, a man one foot tall with a beard thirty feet long who carried an iron club weighing five hundredweight!

Peri-Banu smiled at each demand. With fairy power, she provided the magical pocket tent, sent her enchanted lion-taming perfume to fetch the miraculous water, and summoned her brother Schaibar, a tiny dwarf of colossal strength.

When the Sultan and his wicked councilors drew their scimitars upon Schaibar, the dwarf whirled his iron club, routing the plotters and ending the reign of deceit. Ahmad was crowned Sultan, ruling with benevolence, accompanied by Peri-Banu whose wisdom brought peace and prosperity to the empire for decades.
moral: True worth is proven through devotion and integrity, while magical wonders pale before sincere affection and civic duty.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Prince Ahmad and the Fairy Peri-Banu"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
